CAS Monograph 3, *Stochastic Loss Reserving Using Generalized Linear Models*
(Greg Taylor and Gráinne McGuire, 2016), shows that the chain ladder is a
generalized linear model, uses that fact to put a prediction error on the
reserve, checks the model with residuals, and then improves on it with fewer
parameters and a few interactions. Every example runs on one triangle. This
guide runs those examples in prospicio from R and prints the monograph's
numbers next to prospicio's.

This is the R twin of the Python guide
[`reserving-taylor-mcguire.md`](reserving-taylor-mcguire.md): the same
sections, the same models and the same numbers. The R package calls the same
Rust code as the Python one, and the designs below have the same columns in
the same order as the Python guide's, so the estimates and even the seeded simulations agree with
the Python guide to every digit printed.

The text of the monograph is the authors'; what follows explains it in new
words with the numbers recomputed. Table and figure numbers are the
monograph's. Money is in thousands of dollars, as in the monograph. For which
reserving method to pick in general, read
[`reserving-methods.md`](reserving-methods.md).

Two parts of prospicio carry the work: `triangle()`, `chain_ladder()`,
`mack()`, `odp_bootstrap()` and `odp_glm()` on the triangle, and `glm_fit()`
for the one model that is not on the triangle's cells, the ODP Mack model of
section 2. `odp_glm()` fits the monograph's models to the incremental cells and
gives their analytic prediction error, simulated reserves and residual
diagnostics. By default it fits the cross-classified model; its `formula`
argument takes any other design written on the cells of `odp_glm_cells()`, so
every model in the monograph's chapter 7 is the same call with another
formula.

Each R chunk is followed by the text it prints.
`R/prospicio/tests/test-guides.R` runs the chunks in order and requires each
one to print exactly that text. To render the page, install the R package and
run `quarto render docs/guides/reserving-taylor-mcguire.qmd`.

```{r}
#| label: setup
library(prospicio)

# Thousands separators, as Python's {:,.0f}.
comma <- function(x, digits = 0) {
  formatC(round(x, digits), format = "f", digits = digits, big.mark = ",")
}
```

## 1. The data and the chain ladder

The monograph's example (Table 1-1) is the incremental paid loss triangle of a
New Jersey workers compensation insurer, accident years 1988 to 1997, from
Meyers and Shi's (2011) database, chosen because its age-to-age factors are
nearly constant down each column.

```{r}
INCREMENTS <- list( # Table 1-1, accident years 1988 to 1997, development years 1 to 10
  c(41821, 34729, 20147, 15965, 11285, 5924, 4775, 3742, 3435, 2958),
  c(48167, 39495, 24444, 18178, 10840, 7379, 5683, 4758, 3959),
  c(52058, 47459, 27359, 17916, 11448, 8846, 5869, 5391),
  c(57251, 49510, 27036, 20871, 14304, 10552, 7742),
  c(59213, 54129, 29566, 22484, 14114, 10000),
  c(59475, 52076, 26836, 22332, 14756),
  c(65607, 44648, 27062, 22655),
  c(56748, 39315, 26748),
  c(52212, 40030),
  c(43962)
)
K <- length(INCREMENTS)
YEARS <- 1988:1997
cumulative <- lapply(INCREMENTS, cumsum)
long <- data.frame(
  year = rep(YEARS, lengths(cumulative)),
  age = unlist(lapply(lengths(cumulative), function(n) 12 * seq_len(n))),
  paid = unlist(cumulative)
)
tri <- triangle(long, "year", "age", "paid")
cl <- chain_ladder(tri, "paid")
cat("factors ", sprintf("%.3f", cl@ldf), "\n")
cat("reserves", round(cl@reserve[-1]), "\n")
cat("total   ", round(cl@total_reserve), "\n")
```

```text
factors  1.815 1.261 1.158 1.088 1.055 1.039 1.030 1.025 1.021
reserves 3398 8155 14579 22645 31865 45753 60093 80983 105874
total    373346
```

The volume-weighted factors are Table 3-1 and the reserves by accident year
are the last column of Table 3-2, 3,398 for 1989 up to 105,874 for 1997, with a
total of 373,346. They match to the unit.

## 2. The chain ladder as a GLM

The *cross-classified* ODP model makes each incremental payment `Y[k, j]`
over-dispersed Poisson with mean `a[k] * b[j]` and variance `phi` times the
mean: a GLM with a log link and one indicator column per accident year and per
development year, with `ln b[1] = 0` to make the design full rank.

`odp_glm(tri, "paid")` fits this model as it stands, coded with an intercept
and origin and development factors measured from the first of each. To print
the monograph's coding, one `ln a[k]` per accident year and no intercept, the
formula says so. `odp_glm_cells()` gives the triangle's 100 cells, the 55
observed and the 45 to forecast, in the order the formula is evaluated on, with
each cell's accident and development year as a 0-based index. A formula looks
up the variables it does not find in the cells in its own environment, so the
1-based `k` and `j` are defined once here:

```{r}
cells <- odp_glm_cells(tri, "paid")
k <- cells$origin_index + 1 # accident year, 1 to 10
j <- cells$development_index + 1 # development year, 1 to 10
cc <- odp_glm(tri, "paid", formula = ~ 0 + factor(k) + factor(j))
est <- cc@coefficients
se <- cc@std_errors
cat(" j or k   ln a    s.e.    ln b    s.e.\n")
cat(sprintf("%6d %7.3f %7.4f   0.000\n", 1, est[1], se[1]))
for (i in 2:K) {
  cat(sprintf("%6d %7.3f %7.4f %7.3f %7.4f\n", i, est[i], se[i], est[K + i - 1], se[K + i - 1]))
}
cat(sprintf("phi %.1f on %.0f degrees of freedom\n", cc@dispersion, sum(cells$observed) - length(est)))
```

```text
 j or k   ln a    s.e.    ln b    s.e.
     1  10.657  0.0316   0.000
     2  10.795  0.0299  -0.205  0.0228
     3  10.899  0.0289  -0.747  0.0282
     4  10.989  0.0281  -1.017  0.0328
     5  11.039  0.0278  -1.452  0.0421
     6  11.016  0.0285  -1.833  0.0547
     7  11.008  0.0295  -2.140  0.0715
     8  10.891  0.0327  -2.348  0.0931
     9  10.836  0.0367  -2.513  0.1267
    10  10.691  0.0510  -2.664  0.1993
phi 114.5 on 36 degrees of freedom
```

This is Table 5-1 (and the first columns of Table 3-5) digit for digit, and
the monograph's scale parameter of 114.5: Pearson's chi-square over the
55 - 19 = 36 residual degrees of freedom, which `odp_glm()` uses. Rescaled so the `b[j]` sum to 1, `a[k]` is the ultimate and `b[j]` the
payment pattern (Table 3-3), and the future cells summed by year are the chain
ladder's reserves:

```{r}
a <- exp(est[1:K])
b <- exp(c(0, est[(K + 1):(2 * K - 1)]))
cat("a (ultimates)", round(a * sum(b)), "\n")
cat("b (pattern)  ", sprintf("%.3f", b / sum(b)), "\n")
cat("GLM reserves ", round(cc@reserves[-1]), round(cc@total_reserve), "\n")
cat("largest gap to the chain ladder below 1e-6:", max(abs(cc@reserves[-1] - cl@reserve[-1])) < 1e-6, "\n")
```

```text
a (ultimates) 144781 166301 184501 201845 212151 207340 205725 182904 173225 149836
b (pattern)   0.293 0.239 0.139 0.106 0.069 0.047 0.035 0.028 0.024 0.020
GLM reserves  3398 8155 14579 22645 31865 45753 60093 80983 105874 373346
largest gap to the chain ladder below 1e-6: TRUE
```

The GLM and the chain ladder are the same estimator here: maximum likelihood
under the ODP equates the fitted and actual total of every row and column,
which is what the chain ladder preserves too (the monograph's chapter 3).

The *ODP Mack* model works on the age-to-age factors: each `f[k, j] - 1` is
ODP with mean `f[j] - 1` and prior weight the cumulative paid `X[k, j]`. Its
cells are the age-to-age links, not the triangle's increments, so it is fitted
with `glm_fit()`, where `dispersion = "pearson"` makes the Poisson
over-dispersed.

```{r}
links <- do.call(rbind, lapply(1:(K - 1), function(k) data.frame(k = k, j = seq_len(K - k))))
growth <- mapply(function(k, j) cumulative[[k]][j + 1] / cumulative[[k]][j] - 1, links$k, links$j)
weight <- mapply(function(k, j) cumulative[[k]][j], links$k, links$j)
md <- data.frame(growth = growth, j = factor(links$j))
odp_mack <- glm_fit(growth ~ 0 + j, md, family = "poisson", link = "log",
                    weights = weight, dispersion = "pearson")
cat("f - 1", sprintf("%.3f", exp(odp_mack@coefficients)), "\n")
```

```text
f - 1 0.815 0.261 0.158 0.088 0.055 0.039 0.030 0.025 0.021
```

These are Table 3-4, the chain-ladder factors less one. Both models give the
same forecast but not the same prediction error (section 4).

## 3. Prediction error by the delta method

The MSEP of a sum of future cells is process error, `phi` times their mean,
plus parameter error `g' Sigma g`, with `g = sum of mu * x` over the cells and
`Sigma` the coefficients' covariance (the monograph's (5-11) to (5-13)). The
fit's `prediction_error` does it for each accident year and the total,
whatever the design.

```{r}
pe <- cc@prediction_error[-1, ] # a row per accident year 1989 to 1997, then Total
TABLE_5_4 <- rbind( # forecast, RMSEP, CVP %
  c(3398, 924, 27.2), c(8155, 1363, 16.7), c(14579, 1775, 12.2), c(22645, 2169, 9.6),
  c(31865, 2523, 7.9), c(45753, 3036, 6.6), c(60093, 3577, 6.0), c(80983, 4538, 5.6),
  c(105874, 6786, 6.4), c(373346, 14076, 3.8)
)
cat("year    forecast  RMSEP   CVP |  book: forecast  RMSEP   CVP\n")
for (i in 1:K) {
  cat(sprintf("%-6s %9s %6s %5.1f |  %12s %6s %5.1f\n", pe$origin[i],
              comma(pe$reserve[i]), comma(pe$rmsep[i]), 100 * pe$cv[i],
              comma(TABLE_5_4[i, 1]), comma(TABLE_5_4[i, 2]), TABLE_5_4[i, 3]))
}
```

```text
year    forecast  RMSEP   CVP |  book: forecast  RMSEP   CVP
1989       3,398    924  27.2 |         3,398    924  27.2
1990       8,155  1,363  16.7 |         8,155  1,363  16.7
1991      14,579  1,775  12.2 |        14,579  1,775  12.2
1992      22,645  2,169   9.6 |        22,645  2,169   9.6
1993      31,865  2,523   7.9 |        31,865  2,523   7.9
1994      45,753  3,036   6.6 |        45,753  3,036   6.6
1995      60,093  3,577   6.0 |        60,093  3,577   6.0
1996      80,983  4,538   5.6 |        80,983  4,538   5.6
1997     105,874  6,786   6.4 |       105,874  6,786   6.4
Total    373,346 14,076   3.8 |       373,346 14,076   3.8
```

Every number in Table 5-4 matches. The split, and the total if the years were
independent:

```{r}
cat(sprintf("process   %7s\n", comma(pe$process_se[K])))
cat(sprintf("parameter %7s\n", comma(pe$parameter_se[K])))
by_year_msep <- pe$rmsep[-K]^2
cat(sprintf("total if the years were independent %7s  (book 10,275)\n", comma(sqrt(sum(by_year_msep)))))
```

```text
process     6,539
parameter  12,465
total if the years were independent  10,275  (book 10,275)
```

The parameter error dominates, and the years are positively correlated: they
share the development-year parameters.

## 4. Prediction error by simulation

The monograph's parametric bootstrap (section 5.4.2) draws the coefficients
from their normal approximation and adds process error, 10,000 times.
`predict_distribution()` of an `odp_glm()` fit with `parameters = "normal"`
does that, with process error `phi * Poisson(mu / phi)`; its columns are the
future cells of the fit's `future`, summed here by accident year.

```{r}
by_year_draws <- function(fit, seed, n_sims = 10000) {
  pd <- predict_distribution(fit, n_sims = n_sims, seed = seed, parameters = "normal")
  m <- draw_matrix(pd) # one row per draw, one column per future cell
  sapply(split(seq_len(ncol(m)), fit@future$origin), function(i) rowSums(m[, i, drop = FALSE]))
}
show <- function(sims, book) {
  cat("year    mean    RMSEP   CVP |  book: mean   RMSEP   CVP\n")
  sims <- cbind(sims, rowSums(sims))
  for (i in 1:K) {
    m <- mean(sims[, i])
    e <- stats::sd(sims[, i])
    cat(sprintf("%-6s %8s %7s %5.1f |  %9s %7s %5.1f\n", if (i < K) YEARS[i + 1] else "Total",
                comma(m), comma(e), 100 * e / m, comma(book[i, 1]), comma(book[i, 2]), book[i, 3]))
  }
}
TABLE_5_5 <- rbind(
  c(3476, 937, 27.0), c(8269, 1366, 16.5), c(14738, 1794, 12.2), c(22776, 2186, 9.6),
  c(32043, 2525, 7.9), c(45963, 3057, 6.7), c(60273, 3608, 6.0), c(81249, 4589, 5.6),
  c(106204, 6831, 6.4), c(374992, 14286, 3.8)
)
show(by_year_draws(cc, seed = 1), TABLE_5_5)
```

```text
year    mean    RMSEP   CVP |  book: mean   RMSEP   CVP
1989      3,467     943  27.2 |      3,476     937  27.0
1990      8,290   1,397  16.8 |      8,269   1,366  16.5
1991     14,725   1,792  12.2 |     14,738   1,794  12.2
1992     22,792   2,177   9.6 |     22,776   2,186   9.6
1993     32,037   2,528   7.9 |     32,043   2,525   7.9
1994     45,950   3,101   6.7 |     45,963   3,057   6.7
1995     60,313   3,593   6.0 |     60,273   3,608   6.0
1996     81,254   4,582   5.6 |     81,249   4,589   5.6
1997    106,056   6,849   6.5 |    106,204   6,831   6.4
Total   374,883  14,432   3.8 |    374,992  14,286   3.8
```

The results agree with Table 5-5 within simulation noise (a standard deviation
from 10,000 draws carries a relative error of about 0.7%). Both sets of means
sit above the chain ladder: drawing `beta` from a normal and taking
`exp(x' beta)` gives each cell the mean `mu * exp(v / 2)`, with `v = x' Sigma x`,
the lognormal bias. The fit's `future` has it cell by cell, as
`predictive_mean`:

```{r}
cat(sprintf("chain ladder %9s\n", comma(cc@total_reserve)))
cat(sprintf("E[simulated] %9s   (book's bootstrap mean 374,992)\n", comma(sum(cc@future$predictive_mean))))
```

```text
chain ladder   373,346
E[simulated]   374,994   (book's bootstrap mean 374,992)
```

The monograph puts the higher means down to sampling error; the bias accounts
for the whole gap. `parameters = "mean_preserving"` simulates around the chain
ladder's forecast instead.

The England-Verrall ODP bootstrap and Mack's model answer the same question
with other assumptions:

```{r}
ob <- odp_bootstrap(tri, "paid", n_sims = 10000, seed = 1)
boot_total <- rowSums(draw_matrix(ob@reserves))
mk <- mack(tri, "paid")
cat(sprintf("ODP bootstrap scale %.1f\n", ob@scale))
cat(sprintf("ODP bootstrap total mean %9s  RMSEP %7s\n", comma(mean(boot_total)), comma(stats::sd(boot_total))))
cat(sprintf("Mack total               %9s  RMSEP %7s\n", comma(mk@total_reserve), comma(mk@total_standard_error)))
cat("Mack by year", round(mk@standard_error[-1]), "\n")
```

```text
ODP bootstrap scale 114.5
ODP bootstrap total mean   373,105  RMSEP  14,194
Mack total                 373,346  RMSEP  10,939
Mack by year 39 44 410 850 1364 1959 2308 3179 9192
```

The ODP bootstrap uses the same Pearson `phi` and lands close to the parametric
bootstrap. Mack's total standard error is about a quarter lower, and tiny for
the older years: on this triangle the age-to-age factors barely scatter in the
later columns, while the ODP ties every payment's variance to its size through
one `phi`. Same forecast, different prediction error.

## 5. Residual diagnostics

The standardized deviance residual divides a cell's deviance residual by
`sqrt(phi * (1 - h))`, with `h` its leverage. The fit's `residuals` has them
for every observed cell, and `residual_summary()` groups them by development
year, accident year or calendar year:

```{r}
dev <- residual_summary(cc, "development")
cal <- residual_summary(cc, "calendar")
cat("by development year 1 to 8, spread (sd) of the residuals\n")
cat(sprintf("%.2f", dev$sd[1:8]), "\n")
cat("by calendar year 1988 to 1997, mean residual\n")
cat(sprintf("%+.2f", cal$mean), "\n")
```

```text
by development year 1 to 8, spread (sd) of the residuals
1.42 1.68 0.94 0.67 0.91 0.86 0.75 0.49
by calendar year 1988 to 1997, mean residual
-0.38 -0.13 -0.40 +0.56 +0.42 -0.43 +0.23 -0.27 -0.26 +0.32
```

The spreads are sample standard deviations, divisor `n - 1`; an earlier
version of this guide divided by `n`, which printed each 6% to 18% lower (1.34
for development year 1, 0.40 for year 8). The residuals and the calendar-year
means are unchanged. The two corner cells (1988's last year, 1997's first)
have leverage one and no residual. Development years 1 and 2 scatter more than the later ones (the
monograph's Figure 6-19) and the calendar-year means swing from negative to
positive (its Figure 6-20). The ratio of actual to fitted by cell is the
monograph's heat map, Figure 6-22:

```{r}
heat_map <- function(fit) {
  r <- fit@residuals
  for (year in YEARS) {
    cat(year, sprintf("%4d", round(100 * r$actual_to_fitted[r$origin == year])), "\n")
  }
}
heat_map(cc)
```

```text
1988   98  100  100  104  113   87   96   92  100  100
1989   99   99  106  103   95   95   99  102  100
1990   96  108  107   91   90  102   92  104
1991   97  103   96   97  103  111  111
1992   95  107  100  100   97  100
1993   98  105   93  101  104
1994  109   91   95  104
1995  106   90  105
1996  103   97
1997  100
```

In development year 1 the early accident years are below 100% and the later
ones above, and development year 2 runs the other way: the payment pattern has
shifted, an interaction the cross-classified model cannot express.

## 6. Fewer parameters

Chapter 7 replaces the ten `ln a[k]` by a quadratic in `k` (model 7-2), then
the development effects by a straight line in `j` with a kink at 7.5 plus a
term for development year 2 (model 7-10), and adds the interactions the heat
map pointed to (model 7-14). Each is the same call with another formula:

```{r}
quad <- odp_glm(tri, "paid", formula = ~ 0 + k + I(k^2) + factor(j))
q <- quad@coefficients
level <- q[[3]]
cat(sprintf("accident year effect %.3f + %.4f k %.4f k^2  (book 10.471 + 0.2001 k - 0.0179 k^2)\n",
            level, q[[1]], q[[2]]))
cat("ln b - ln b1", sprintf("%.3f", q[4:12] - level), "\n")
cat("book        ", sprintf("%.3f", c(-0.206, -0.750, -1.015, -1.452, -1.830, -2.142, -2.353, -2.514, -2.661)), "\n")
```

```text
accident year effect 10.471 + 0.2001 k -0.0179 k^2  (book 10.471 + 0.2001 k - 0.0179 k^2)
ln b - ln b1 -0.206 -0.750 -1.015 -1.452 -1.830 -2.142 -2.353 -2.514 -2.661
book         -0.206 -0.750 -1.015 -1.452 -1.830 -2.142 -2.353 -2.514 -2.661
```

```{r}
early <- as.numeric(k <= 6) # accident years 1 to 6
smooth <- odp_glm(tri, "paid", formula = ~ k + I(k^2) + I(j - 1) + I(pmax(0, j - 7.5)) + I(1 * (j == 2)))
interact <- odp_glm(tri, "paid", formula = ~ k + I(k^2) + I(j - 1) + I(pmax(0, j - 7.5)) + I(1 * (j == 2)) +
                      I(1 * (j == 4)) + I((j == 1) * early) + I((j == 2) * early) + I((j == 3) * k))
cat("model 7-10  ", sprintf("%7.4f", smooth@coefficients), "\n")
cat("Table 7-3   ", sprintf("%7.3f", c(10.469, 0.200, -0.018, -0.358, 0.236, 0.155)), "\n")
cat("model 7-14  ", sprintf("%7.4f", interact@coefficients), "\n")
cat("Table 7-5   ", sprintf("%7.4f", c(10.4900, 0.2066, -0.0183, -0.3685, 0.2720, 0.0375, 0.0528,
                                       -0.0671, 0.1273, -0.0113)), "\n")
cat(sprintf("phi: 7-2 %.1f, 7-10 %.1f, 7-14 %.1f\n", quad@dispersion, smooth@dispersion, interact@dispersion))
```

```text
model 7-10   10.4687  0.2001 -0.0179 -0.3577  0.2356  0.1545
Table 7-3     10.469   0.200  -0.018  -0.358   0.236   0.155
model 7-14   10.4904  0.2066 -0.0183 -0.3685  0.2720  0.0375  0.0528 -0.0671  0.1273 -0.0113
Table 7-5    10.4900  0.2066 -0.0183 -0.3685  0.2720  0.0375  0.0528 -0.0671  0.1273 -0.0113
phi: 7-2 102.6, 7-10 107.3, 7-14 53.9
```

All match Tables 7-1, 7-3 and 7-5. Model 7-10's `c` is 0.1544995, a hair below
0.1545, which Table 7-3 rounds to 0.155: SAS's estimate needs to differ only in
the seventh decimal. The scale falls from 114.5 to about 54 with the
interactions. The six-parameter model's heat map is Figure 7-5:

```{r}
heat_map(smooth)
```

```text
1988   99  101   98  111  112   84   97   96  100   97
1989   99   99  102  109   93   90   99  106   99
1990   95  107  102   96   88   97   92  107
1991   97  103   94  104  102  107  113
1992   97  108   99  108   97   98
1993   97  104   89  106  101
1994  110   92   93  112
1995  102   87   99
1996  105   98
1997  101
```

## 7. Forecasts and prediction error of the smaller models

The delta method of section 3 applies to any design (the `Total` row of
`prediction_error`); the parametric bootstrap is the monograph's Tables 7-2,
7-4 and 7-6.

```{r}
BOOK <- list("7-2 quadratic" = c(373641, 13086), "7-10 smooth" = c(373403, 13248),
             "7-14 interactions" = c(371559, 10907))
models <- list(quad, smooth, interact)
cat("model              delta: forecast  RMSEP | bootstrap: mean  RMSEP |  book: mean  RMSEP\n")
for (i in seq_along(BOOK)) {
  fit <- models[[i]]
  delta <- fit@prediction_error[K + 1, ] # the Total row
  total <- rowSums(by_year_draws(fit, seed = 1))
  cat(sprintf("%-18s %15s %6s | %15s %6s | %10s %6s\n", names(BOOK)[i], comma(delta$reserve), comma(delta$rmsep),
              comma(mean(total)), comma(stats::sd(total)), comma(BOOK[[i]][1]), comma(BOOK[[i]][2])))
}
```

```text
model              delta: forecast  RMSEP | bootstrap: mean  RMSEP |  book: mean  RMSEP
7-2 quadratic              372,532 13,030 |         373,866 13,131 |    373,641 13,086
7-10 smooth                373,006 13,215 |         373,675 13,392 |    373,403 13,248
7-14 interactions          370,493 11,021 |         370,965 11,135 |    371,559 10,907
```

```{r}
TABLE_7_6 <- rbind(
  c(3630, 569, 15.7), c(8557, 935, 10.9), c(14563, 1203, 8.3), c(22193, 1418, 6.4),
  c(32505, 1677, 5.2), c(45771, 2018, 4.4), c(62998, 2459, 3.9), c(79601, 3079, 3.9),
  c(101742, 4094, 4.0), c(371559, 10907, 2.9)
)
show(by_year_draws(interact, seed = 1), TABLE_7_6)
```

1989      3,635     560  15.4 |      3,630     569  15.7
1990      8,573     937  10.9 |      8,557     935  10.9

The bootstraps agree with the monograph within noise. The quadratic
accident-year effect cuts the total RMSEP from about 14,100 to 13,000, the
smooth development pattern gives a little back, and the interactions bring it
to about 11,000, a CV near 3%.

## 8. Choosing between the models

Table 7-7's AIC and BIC use the Poisson kernel `sum(y log(mu) - mu) / phi` with
`phi` held at the interaction model's value; GCV is `n * RSS / (n - p)^2` with
raw residuals.

```{r}
y <- cc@residuals$actual # the 55 observed increments
n <- length(y)
phi_fixed <- interact@dispersion
TABLE_7_7 <- rbind(c(-509392, -509354, 6685428), c(-509400, -509376, 5075351),
                   c(-509397, -509385, 4311874), c(-509441, -509421, 1733202))
labels <- c("chain ladder", "7-2 quadratic", "7-10 smooth", "7-14 interactions")
cat("model                  AIC        BIC       GCV |  book:  AIC        BIC       GCV\n")
for (i in 1:4) {
  fit <- list(cc, quad, smooth, interact)[[i]]
  mu <- fit@residuals$fitted
  p <- length(fit@coefficients)
  loglik <- sum(y * log(mu) - mu) / phi_fixed
  gcv <- n * sum((y - mu)^2) / (n - p)^2
  cat(sprintf("%-18s %10s %10s %9s | %10s %10s %9s\n", labels[i], comma(-2 * loglik + 2 * p),
              comma(-2 * loglik + p * log(n)), comma(gcv),
              comma(TABLE_7_7[i, 1]), comma(TABLE_7_7[i, 2]), comma(TABLE_7_7[i, 3])))
}
```

```text
model                  AIC        BIC       GCV |  book:  AIC        BIC       GCV
chain ladder         -509,391   -509,353 6,685,459 |   -509,392   -509,354 6,685,428
7-2 quadratic        -509,399   -509,375 5,075,358 |   -509,400   -509,376 5,075,351
7-10 smooth          -509,396   -509,384 4,311,876 |   -509,397   -509,385 4,311,874
7-14 interactions    -509,440   -509,420 1,733,200 |   -509,441   -509,421 1,733,202
```

GCV agrees to five significant figures; AIC and BIC sit 0.7 to 1.4 above the
printed values, a relative `2e-6` of a log-likelihood near 254,700 (the level
of `phi` or SAS's convergence), while the differences between models agree, so
the ranking is the monograph's.

## 9. A gamma cross-classified model

A gamma error, variance proportional to the mean squared, is one argument
away, `family = "gamma"` (or `"tweedie"` with a `power` between 1 and 2), here
on the default cross-classified design. The monograph prints no gamma results
for this triangle.

```{r}
gamma <- odp_glm(tri, "paid", family = "gamma")
cat(sprintf("gamma phi %.4f\n", gamma@dispersion))
cat("gamma reserves", round(gamma@reserves[-1]), "\n")
cat(sprintf("gamma total %s  (chain ladder %s)\n", comma(gamma@total_reserve), comma(cc@total_reserve)))
```

```text
gamma phi 0.0047
gamma reserves 3423 8134 15086 22667 31820 45434 60216 80829 105857
gamma total 373,466  (chain ladder 373,346)
```

The gamma fit no longer preserves the row and column totals, so its forecasts
are close to, but not, the chain ladder's. Its `prediction_error` uses the
process variance `phi * mu^2`.

## 10. What matched, and what the R package cannot do yet

The matches and differences are those of the Python guide: Tables 3-1 to 3-5,
5-1, 5-4, 7-1, 7-3 and 7-5 and the heat maps exactly; the bootstraps within
noise, with means raised by the lognormal bias; Table 7-7 within about one unit.

**Gaps closed since this guide was first written.** Earlier versions built
the design matrices, the delta-method MSEP, the standardized residuals and the
heat map by hand. The library now does all of them, and the guide uses it:
`odp_glm()` fits the cross-classified ODP and, through `formula` on the cells
of `odp_glm_cells()`, any other design (models 7-2, 7-10 and 7-14); the fit's
`prediction_error` gives the delta-method MSEP by accident year and in total
(Table 5-4); `predict_distribution()` and the `future` cells'
`predictive_mean` the parametric bootstrap and its lognormal bias; the
`residuals` and `residual_summary()` the standardized residuals and the heat
maps; and `family =` and `power =` a gamma or Tweedie error. What is still
written out here is only the monograph's own: each model's formula, the ODP
Mack model of section 2 (a `glm_fit()` on the age-to-age factors, which are
not the triangle's cells) and the information criteria of Table 7-7, whose
log-likelihood the monograph defines with a fixed `phi`. For a `glm_fit()`
model, `glm_diagnostics()` gives residuals, hat values and Cook's distances,
and `prediction_se()` and `sum_prediction_error()` the standard errors of a
prediction and of a sum of predictions.
